events.title: Graduate Workshop Series | History, Memory, Research, and Creative Practice with Dr. Haekyoung Lee
events.summary: This is a 5-part Graduate Workshop Series led by Dr. Haekyoung Lee, Professor Emerita of Theater Arts at Kookmin University. Designed for graduate students across disciplines, this series explores modern Korean history, archival methodology, public history, and creative practice. Dr. Lee is a professor emerita at the Department of Theater Arts, at Kookmin University, in Seoul, South Korea. She is a scholar and practitioner in modern Korean theatre and performance, with research interests in modern Korean history, transpacific cultural and institutional networks, diaspora, documentary performance, and archival methodology. Recent work explores the historical connections between the University of Michigan and modern Korea, with particular attention to Ilhan New, Korean diasporic networks, and historically grounded performance. events.title: The Tree of Eternity
events.summary: The Tree of Eternity is an immersive, interactive installation that explores remembrance, loss, and the enduring presence of those we have loved. The installation centers on a projected tree surrounded by interactive terminal pods that control its structure. Visitors approach interactive pods positioned throughout the gallery space, where they are invited to recall memories of people or experiences throughout their lives. Depending on the kiosk they interact with, different effects will be present on the projected tree. As more visitors’ memories are inputted, the tree’s visuals adapt and change form, demonstrating that our memories persist with us. Projection mapping creates ethereal visuals accompanied by atmospheric audio. Even when visitors aren't actively engaging with the kiosks, the system generates ambient transmissions, suggesting that the tree—and the memories it embodies—continues to live and grow. The installation creates a dialogue between life and death, presence and absence, individual memory and collective remembrance, inviting participants to contribute to a living memorial that persists beyond any single moment of grief or reflection.

events.title: GalleryDAAS presents Women Warriors of the African Diaspora
events.summary: GalleryDAAS is pleased to present an exhibit focused on women warriors of the African Diaspora, both conventional and nonconventional, including legends such as Harriet Tubman, Audre Lorde, Wangari Maathai, Zora Neale Hurston, Nanny of the Maroons and Hatshepsut. "There was one of two things I had a right to: liberty or death. If I could not have one, I would take the other, for no man should take me alive. I should fight for liberty as long as my strength lasted.”- Harriet Tubman What constitutes a warrior? The word brings to mind someone skilled, experienced, and engaged in combat or military service, such as a soldier or protector in past and present tribal, feudal, or national armies, such as the intimidating Mino of Dahomey (present-day Benin), the inspiration for the movie The Woman King, or the valiant revolutionary Solitude of Guadeloupe. The term also applies to those who show great courage, resilience, or determination in the face of personal challenges, such as illness, as exemplified by Audre Lorde, an author, librarian, and activist who wrote The Cancer Journals. The term additionally describes dedicated advocates for a cause, such as the political activist and educator Angela Davis or the environmental activist Wangari Maathai. Many societies also uphold the role of community protectors, providers, and keepers of peace and culture, like multimedia artist and activist Betye Saar or Zora Neale Hurston, anthropologist, author, and documentary filmmaker. And then there are the legends. Harriet Tubman, the famous abolitionist and activist, escaped enslavement in Maryland by traveling over 90 miles to Philadelphia, then returned 13 more times to lead others to freedom. Many are not aware of her involvement during the Civil War as a Union spy and, more importantly, serving as a key intelligence network leader, scout, pilot, and the first woman to lead an armed U.S. military operation by guiding the Combahee River Raid, a daring American Civil War operation in South Carolina. DAAS alumna (‘26) Madysen Casey kindly contributed original multimedia pieces that portray an array of unconventional women warriors along with her personal reflections about them. Our new Gallery Manager, Symone Campbell, was instrumental in creating her first exhibit, and Rebecca Jackson, DAAS’ Communications Coordinator, once again used her incredible skills to design the exhibit, assist with editing, and create our publicity. Our formidable DAAS crew exemplified the resilience of women warriors. We hope these incredible conventional and unconventional warriors become your North stars - your guides - as they have been ours throughout the curatorial process. May their legacies, their words, their images remind you that you can be a bright light even in the face of what feels like insurmountable darkness. May they inspire you to be fearless and to “jump at de’ sun,” as Zora’s mother advised her. “I am my best work – a series of road maps, reports, recipes, doodles, and prayers from the front lines.” -Audre Lorde

events.title: Like the flowing river
events.summary: Artist Tomoyuki Ueno creates individual works and installations where nature appears to be in an endless conversation with form, one echoing the other, a repetition. They are a combination of certainty and ephemerality, as if hinged between living and loss. The specificity of Ueno’s sculptural works reads like poetry. Ueno’s installation offers visitors time away, for contemplation, to draw inward, to come inside, to ask the question, “How are art and the everyday intertwined?” Honoring the Buddhist philosophy of impermanence, one becomes a continuation of the other. The artist intends the space to offer a restorative and meditative experience. This exhibition includes artworks created from natural materials foraged by the artist while in artist residency in Ann Arbor. *The title refers to the opening line of Hōjōki, written by 13th-century Japanese Buddhist monk Kamo no Chōmei: "The flow of the river is ceaseless, and the water is never the same…"*

events.title: cART-ography: An Arts, Culture, and Sustainability Workshop
events.summary: Countermapping is a radical way to use the tools of mapping in a way that engages with our environment in a politically explicit way. It can bring to light hidden histories of structural environmental discrimination, subvert dominant claims about space, and highlight ongoing struggles for decolonization and justice. In this workshop, we’ll think about the political dimensions of mapping, geography, and the environment, especially in the local context. Then, we’ll create our own countermaps using collage, a fun medium friendly to all levels of artistic experience. Plus, dinner is provided!

events.title: THEATRE l She Kills Monsters
events.summary: Planet Ant Theatre presents SHE KILLS MONSTERS by Qui Nguyen, December 4-19, 2026, at Ant Hall. When Agnes Evans loses her teenage sister Tilly, she realizes she barely knew her. Tilly's Dungeons & Dragons notebook pulls Agnes into a fantastical world of epic quests, homicidal fairies, snarling ogres, and 90s pop culture as she tries to reconnect with her sister and find the courage she never knew she had. Equal parts comedy, heartfelt drama, and action-packed adventure, the play celebrates the power of great storytelling and the geek and warrior in all of us. Content advisory: Strong language, stage combat, sexual references, and themes of grief, bullying, and suicide. Recommended for ages 13+. She Kills Monsters is presented by arrangement with Concord Theatricals on behalf of Samuel French, Inc. For more information, visit www.concordtheatricals.com.

featuredEvents.title: The American G Bugle: Music and Innovations from 1892-1976
featuredEvents.summary: Explore the evolution of the G bugle through historical insights, live demonstrations, and performances. Tubist Wesley DeCasere will discuss the instrument's technological advancements and its changing role in American musical life.

evidence.description: How did a niche valveless instrument evolve into a widespread, versatile musical voice? Through historical insights, live demonstrations, and performances using instruments from the Stearns Collection and the Marching Pageantry Arts Museum, tubist Wesley DeCasere discusses the G bugle's technological evolution and its changing role in American musical life.

evidence.description: This experimental talk has two parts. In the first 30 mins, I'll explain our proof of the join-meet positivity using geometric Satake. In the last 20 mins, I'll play an AI-generated video of the proof. In the last few minutes, we'll vote on who did a better job: me or the AI.
